candidates.title: Proceedings from the 2025 International Consensus Meeting on Orthopedic Infections: the definition of Shoulder Periprosthetic Joint infection.
candidates.authors_short: Namdari S, Zmistowski B, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) remains one of the greatest diagnostic and treatment challenges facing shoulder surgeons and their patients. A definition for shoulder PJI was established by the 2018 International Consensus Meeting (ICM) on Orthopedic Infections, but the selection and weighting of its minor criteria relied largely on expert opinion. The purpose of this study was to present an updated, evidence-based definition of shoulder PJI generated by the 2025 ICM Shoulder Group. METHODS: The 2025 ICM Shoulder Group, an international panel of shoulder surgeons and infectious disease specialists, used a modified Delphi process informed by 86 systematic reviews and by a predictive statistical model derived from the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) Multicenter Revision Arthroplasty and PJI Group dataset to reconsider the 2018 ICM definition of shoulder PJI, including its major criteria, minor criteria, and diagnostic categories. RESULTS: The delegates voted to eliminate organism virulence from the definition and to retain gross intra-articular purulence and presence of a sinus tract as the two criteria defining Definite PJI. The Minor Criteria were revised to include erythema, unexpected wound drainage, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP), elevated synovial neutrophil percentage, positive frozen section, radiographic humeral osteolysis, intraoperative humeral loosening, and positive culture, each statistically weighted using the predictive model. Non-definite PJI was categorized by summed minor criteria score as High likelihood (≥13 points), Moderate likelihood (7-12 points), Unknown (1-6 points), or No PJI (0 points). The final definition achieved unanimous delegate consensus (51 of 51 delegates; 100% agreement; super majority, strong consensus). CONCLUSIONS: The 2025 ICM definition of shoulder PJI represents an evidence-informed evolution of the 2018 definition, combining statistical modeling of prospective multicenter data with structured expert consensus. The definition is expected to continue to evolve as further shoulder-specific data become available.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large prospective RCT directly addressing a common, debated clinical question (weightbearing after first MTP fusion) with patient-relevant outcomes, published in a specialty journal.
bullets: The 2025 ICM updated the shoulder PJI definition, keeping gross purulence and sinus tract as definite criteria while removing organism virulence and adding weighted minor criteria including ESR, CRP, synovial neutrophil percentage, frozen section, and humeral osteolysis.

Non-definite shoulder PJI is now scored by summing minor criteria points into four categories: High likelihood (13 or more points), Moderate likelihood (7 to 12), Unknown (1 to 6), or No PJI (0 points).

Shoulder arthroplasty surgeons working up a failed implant now have an evidence-based, statistically weighted scoring tool to guide the diagnosis of PJI, replacing the prior expert-opinion-based criteria.

candidates.title: To Walk or Not? A Prospective, Randomised Controlled Trial to Evaluate the Effect of Weightbearing on Patient Outcomes Following First Metatarsophalangeal Joint Fusion.
candidates.authors_short: Purdie SD, Glazebrook HM, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: First metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint arthrodesis is the gold standard surgical treatment of hallux rigidus and severe hallux valgus with osteoarthritis after failed nonoperative management. Despite its common use, postoperative weightbearing protocols vary considerably. To date, no prospective randomised controlled trials have directly compared outcomes between immediate weightbearing as tolerated (WBAT) and non-weightbearing (NWB) using modern fixation techniques. This study aimed to evaluate whether immediate WBAT following first metatarsophalangeal joint arthrodesis leads to differences in patient outcomes compared with traditional non-weightbearing protocols. METHODS: A prospective randomised controlled trial was conducted including 68 patients undergoing isolated first-MTP fusion. Patients were randomly allocated either WBAT or NWB protocols. Standardised surgical technique and fixation (crossed screws or plate) were performed by 2 fellowship-trained foot and ankle surgeons. Primary outcomes were the visual analogue scale (VAS) pain scores and the Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM-activities of daily living [ADL] subscale) functional scores, at 12 months. Secondary outcomes included non-union, complications including infection, wound issues, and patient satisfaction. Statistical analysis used t tests and χ2 or Fisher exact tests, with significance at P < .05. RESULTS: Sixty-eight patients (33 WBAT, 35 NWB) completed follow-up. Both groups demonstrated significant improvements in pain and function at 12 months (P < .001 for both). No statistically significant differences were found between WBAT and NWB groups in VAS pain scores (2.97 ± 2.215 vs 2.54 ± 2.147; P = .423), FAAM scores (81.31 ± 16.028 vs 85.02 ± 18.863; P = .387), or patient satisfaction (8.00 ± 2.76 vs 8.34 ± 2.52; P = .594). Complication rates were comparable, with 1 case of hardware irritation in each group (P = .739). CONCLUSION: Following first-MTP joint fusion, immediate weightbearing is safe and results in similar pain relief, patient satisfaction, and complication rates compared with traditional NWB protocols, although a clinically meaningful functional advantage for NWB could not be excluded. These findings support more permissive postoperative strategies, which may offer benefits for patient mobility, independence, recovery time, and health care resource use that were not directly measured in this trial. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, randomised controlled trial. CLINICALTRIALS: gov ID:NCT04473196.
candidates.score_reasoning: Well-designed RCT from a high-impact journal comparing weightbearing protocols after first MTP fusion with direct practice implications for foot and ankle surgeons.
bullets: Patients who walked immediately after first MTP fusion had the same pain scores, function, and satisfaction at 12 months as those kept non-weightbearing.
Complication and non-union rates were equivalent between groups, supporting immediate weightbearing as a safe option after first MTP fusion with modern fixation.
Surgeons can offer immediate weightbearing after first MTP fusion without compromising outcomes, which may ease recovery and reduce patient dependence on assistive devices.

candidates.title: Cemented Femoral Fixation for Primary Total Hip Arthroplasty in the United States: How Surgeon-Cemented Volume Impacts Failure Risk.
candidates.authors_short: Abrolat JL, Zedan AM, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Although cementless femoral fixation remains the United States (U.S.) standard, recent data shows a decline in exclusive cementless usage from 34 to 14% between 2018 and 2024. Whether surgeon-cemented total hip arthroplasty (THA) volume affects implant survivorship remains unclear in this traditionally low-volume environment. As such, we evaluated the association between surgeon cemented stem volume and risk of all-cause revision. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study used a national database to identify primary THAs with cemented femoral fixation from 2016 to 2020. Surgeons were classified by their five-year cemented stem volume: Group 1 (less than 60 stems) or Group 2 (≥ 60 stems). Patients had a minimum two-year follow-up and were propensity score-matched 1:1 based on demographics and comorbidities. A total of 7,174 matched patients were analyzed (3,587 per cohort). Outcomes were all-cause revision, periprosthetic fracture (PPF), mechanical loosening, periprosthetic joint infection (PJI), and dislocation within five years. RESULTS: Patients treated by Group 1 surgeons had higher rates of all study outcomes. At two years, Group 1 patients had higher odds of all-cause revision (odds ratio (OR) = 2.10; 95% confidence interval: 1.44 to 3.11; P < 0.001). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed revision risk diverged sharply within the first postoperative year and persisted through five years. At two-year follow-up, Group 1 patients had increased risk of PPF (OR = 1.58; P = 0.038), loosening (OR = 2.21; P < 0.001), PJI (OR = 2.19; P < 0.001), and dislocation (OR = 2.51; P < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Low surgeon cemented stem volume is strongly associated with increased risk of revision following cemented THA. While cemented femoral fixation remains a useful alternative for high-risk patients undergoing elective THA, the benefits may be compromised if the surgery is performed by surgeons whose specific volume for this type of fixation is low.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large population-based cohort study from JBJS comparing ORIF vs radial head arthroplasty reoperation rates with robust methodology, directly informing surgical decision-making for a common injury.
bullets: Surgeons who performed fewer than 60 cemented hip stems over five years had twice the revision rate compared to higher-volume surgeons, with risk diverging within the first postoperative year.
Low-volume cemented stem surgeons saw higher rates of fracture, loosening, infection, and dislocation at two years, meaning no single complication drove the difference.
For patients where a cemented femoral stem is indicated, referral to or collaboration with a surgeon who regularly uses cemented fixation may meaningfully reduce revision risk.

candidates.title: Radial Head Arthroplasty for Radial Head Fracture Is Associated with a Lower Rate of Reoperation Than Open Reduction Internal Fixation: A Population-Based Cohort Study.
candidates.authors_short: Carroll PJ, Chang N, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: The purpose of this study was to (1) describe the longitudinal trends and epidemiology in surgical management of radial head fractures and (2) compare the rate of reoperation of open reduction internal fixation (ORIF) to radial head arthroplasty (RHA) in Ontario, Canada. METHODS: All patients aged 16 years and older who sustained a radial head fracture between April 1, 2002 and March 31, 2020 were identified using linked provincial health administrative databases from ICES. Patients undergoing ORIF, RHA or radial head excision for a radial head fracture were followed for subsequent reoperation. An unadjusted competing risk survival analysis was performed to tally the cumulative incidence of all-cause revision procedures. Logistic regression models were constructed to identify the patient-, provider- and fracture-related factors associated with reoperation following ORIF and RHA. RESULTS: A total of 3159 patients underwent surgical management of a radial head fracture during the study period. The majority of patients were female (55.9%). The mean age of patients who underwent ORIF, RHA and excision was 43.9, 51.1, 52.6 years, respectively. The mean (SD) follow-up times were 8.9 (+/- 5.0), 8.4 (+/- 5.0) and 11.0 (+/-5.0) years, respectively. In total, 7.7%, 3.8% and 0.8% experienced reoperation during study follow-up, respectively. At 10 years, the cumulative incidence function (CIF) for ORIF, RHA and excision was 15.8% (95% CI 13.9%-17.7%), 10.4% (95% CI 8.7%-12.3%) and 6.5% (95% CI 4.1%-9.5%), respectively. Gray's test demonstrated a statistically significant difference between groups favouring RHA over ORIF (P < 0.0001). The most frequently performed secondary procedure was removal of hardware (32%). The odds of reoperation among those younger than 40 years of age who had an ORIF increased when surgery was performed overnight (between midnight and 7AM) (P = 0.0008). CONCLUSION: Radial head arthroplasty was associated with a lower rate of reoperation than ORIF following radial head fractures, irrespective of patient age. Among patients younger than 40 years, overnight ORIF was associated with an increased rate of reoperation. Long-term studies are needed to evaluate the durability of these findings, particularly in younger patients. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, Retrospective Cohort Comparison using Large Database, Treatment Study.
candidates.score_reasoning: High-impact JBJS instructional review on endoscopic spine surgery evidence maturity and U.S. adoption barriers, highly relevant to practicing spine surgeons navigating evolving techniques.
bullets: In a population-based study of over 3,000 surgically treated radial head fractures, radial head arthroplasty had a 10-year reoperation rate of 10.4% compared to 15.8% for ORIF.
Arthroplasty showed lower reoperation rates than ORIF regardless of patient age, with hardware removal accounting for nearly one-third of all secondary procedures after fixation.
Among patients under 40 who underwent ORIF, surgery performed overnight was independently associated with higher reoperation rates, suggesting timing of fixation matters in younger patients.

candidates.title: Treatment of Vancouver B2 and B3 Periprosthetic Femoral Fractures Using a Modular Tapered Stem: Survivorship and Radiographic Outcomes at Mean 7.8-Year Follow-Up.
candidates.authors_short: Chaudhry F, Bridger A, et al.
candidates.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Periprosthetic fractures (PPF) of the femur are a frequent complication following total hip arthroplasty (THA). Revision THA using a modular tapered stem is a common treatment strategy for these fractures. The purpose of this study was to report the survivorship and clinical outcomes of revision THA using a modular tapered femoral stem to treat PPF of the femur. METHODS: A total of 46 patients were included from our retrospective review of revision total hip arthroplasties performed for Vancouver B2 and B3 fractures between January 2001 and December 2022. A minimum follow-up of two years was required. Among these patients, 30 (65.2%) were women, the mean age at the time of surgery was 73 years (range, 33 to 93), and the mean follow-up was 7.6 years (range, 2.0 to 22.6). Overall, 67.4% (31 of 46) patients were classified as Vancouver B2 fractures. Kaplan-Meier survivorship analysis was conducted with failure defined as revision surgery for any reason. RESULTS: Kaplan-Meier survivorship due to all-cause failure for patients who underwent revision THA to treat PPF via a modular tapered stem was 95.1% (95% CI [confidence interval]: 88.7 to 100.0) at 15 years with four hips at risk. The overall complication rate was 13.0% (six of 46), which included dislocation (four), infection (one), and iliopsoas tendonitis (one). The overall revision rate was 4.3% (two of 46), with revisions performed for dislocation (one) and infection (one). Overall, 95.2% (40 of 42) of patients were ambulatory at final follow-up. CONCLUSION: Our study suggests revision THA using a modular tapered femoral stem for Vancouver B2 and B3 PPF of the femur is a viable treatment option, providing excellent 10- to 15-year survivorship and radiographic outcomes with a low complication rate. Future research should evaluate patient-reported outcomes and longer-term follow-up in larger cohorts.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large national database study examining surgeon cemented THA volume and revision risk, with major practice-level implications as cemented fixation usage increases in the U.S.
bullets: Revision THA using a modular tapered femoral stem for Vancouver B2 and B3 periprosthetic fractures showed 95% implant survival at 15 years in a mean 7.8-year follow-up study of 46 patients.
The overall complication rate was 13%, driven mainly by dislocation, and only 2 of 46 patients required re-revision surgery.
For orthopaedic surgeons managing unstable periprosthetic femoral fractures around a loose stem, modular tapered stems offer durable fixation with a low revision burden at medium-term follow-up.

candidates.title: Defining Long-Term Success After Anatomic Total Shoulder Arthroplasty: Survivorship and Clinically Important Outcomes.
candidates.authors_short: Kucharik MP, Hung V, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Long-term success after anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty (aTSA) is frequently defined by implant survivorship, but revision-free survival may not reflect durable clinical benefit. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study of 791 consecutive aTSAs performed between 2003 and 2015 was conducted. Implant survivorship was assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Clinical outcomes were evaluated at a 10-year landmark, and clinically important thresholds for the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) score were derived using patient satisfaction as the anchor. Multivariable regression identified predictors of revision and substantial clinical benefit (SCB). RESULTS: Kaplan-Meier survivorship was 96.1% at 10 years and 93.7% at 15 years. Walch B glenoid morphology and younger age were independently associated with revision. Clinical outcomes remained improved at long-term follow-up despite gradual attenuation over time. At 10 years, the patient acceptable symptom state (PASS) threshold for the ASES score was 68.1, and 69.5% of shoulders achieved it. The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) and SCB thresholds for the change in ASES score were 14.0 and 39.2, achieved by 79.9% and 55.8% of shoulders, respectively. Younger age, primary glenohumeral osteoarthritis, and lower preoperative ASES score were independently associated with achievement of SCB. CONCLUSIONS: aTSA demonstrated excellent long-term implant survivorship and modest patient-reported outcomes, although shoulder function gradually attenuated over extended follow-up. Despite the gradual functional decline, most patients maintained clinically meaningful benefit at 10 years. Younger age and Walch B morphology increased revision risk. Long-term clinically important thresholds provide patient-centered benchmarks for defining durable success. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic Level III. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.
candidates.score_reasoning: JBJS review challenging established 8-mm overhang threshold for iliopsoas impingement after THA with clinical outcome data, directly changing surgical decision-making in a common THA complication.
bullets: Anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty showed 96% implant survival at 10 years and 94% at 15 years, with younger patients and Walch B glenoid morphology carrying higher revision risk.
At 10 years, about 70% of patients met an acceptable symptom threshold and 56% achieved substantial clinical benefit, though shoulder function declined gradually over time.
Younger age, primary glenohumeral arthritis, and lower preoperative function predicted the greatest long-term patient-reported gains, giving surgeons clearer benchmarks for counseling candidates.

candidates.title: Mechanical Failure and Revision Risk Following Transition from PFNA to TFNA: A Single-Center Cohort Study of 1,970 Patients.
candidates.authors_short: Ben Zoor I, Fogel I, et al.
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare implant mechanical failure, cut-out rate, and time to failure between two cephalomedullary nail designs following an institutional transition. METHODS: Design: Retrospective consecutive cohort study. SETTING: Single Level I trauma center, Israel. PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: Patients aged >65 years with acute OTA/AO 31A fractures (subtypes 31A1-31A3) treated with a short cephalomedullary nail with helical blade fixation, either the Proximal Femoral Nail Antirotation (PFNA) or the Trochanteric Fixation Nail-Advanced (TFNA), between January 2018 and May 2025 were included. Implant type was determined solely by an institutional transition from PFNA to TFNA in March 2023 for logistical reasons rather than surgeon preference. OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: Implant mechanical failure, cut-out rate, time to failure, body mass index (BMI), and Tip-Apex Distance (TAD) were compared between groups. Mortality within the early revision-risk window was compared between groups to exclude survival bias. RESULTS: The PFNA cohort comprised 1,388 patients (mean age 83.1 years, range 65-102; 986 females [71.0%]) and the TFNA cohort 582 patients (mean age 82.9 years, range 65-107; 407 females [69.9%]); baseline demographics were comparable (age, p=0.691; sex, p=0.626). Orthopedic follow-up was 63.9% for the TFNA cohort versus 61.0% for the PFNA cohort (p=0.24), with a shorter maximum observation period for TFNA (TFNA 26 vs. PFNA 88 months).TFNA was associated with a five-fold increase in implant mechanical failure relative to PFNA (TFNA 1.6% vs. PFNA 0.3%; RR=5.36, 95% CI 1.66-17.3; p=0.005), primarily driven by a four-fold increase in cut-outs (1.2% vs. 0.3%; RR=4.18, 95% CI 1.23-14.2; p=0.027). Failures occurred earlier with TFNA (median 80.0 vs. 244.0 days; p=0.027). Among cut-outs, OTA/AO subtype distribution did not differ (31A1: TFNA 57.1% vs. PFNA 50.0%; no 31A3 in either group; p=1.00); TFNA patients had a higher BMI (median 23.9 vs. 20.1 kg/m 2 ; p=0.024), but mean TAD did not differ (TFNA 24.6 vs. PFNA 21.1 mm; p=0.37). Mortality within the revision-risk window did not differ (TFNA 7.2% vs. PFNA 8.8%; p=0.24). CONCLUSIONS: The transition to the Trochanteric Fixation Nail-Advanced (TFNA) was associated with five-fold higher mechanical failure and four-fold higher cut-out rates than the Proximal Femoral Nail Antirotation (PFNA) with earlier failures suggesting reduced mechanical stability of the TFNA during early fracture healing. Heightened vigilance is warranted when using TFNA, particularly in patients with higher body mass index early postoperatively. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic Level III.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large retrospective cohort from CORR evaluating PFNA vs TFNA in 1,970 hip fracture patients, providing high-value implant comparison data relevant to all trauma surgeons treating intertrochanteric fractures.
bullets: In 1,970 patients over 65 with hip fractures, the TFNA had a five-fold higher mechanical failure rate and four-fold higher cut-out rate compared to the PFNA.
Failures with the TFNA occurred earlier (median 80 days versus 244 days), and cut-outs were more common in patients with higher BMI.
Surgeons using the TFNA for intertrochanteric fractures should maintain close early follow-up, especially in heavier patients, given the higher risk of construct failure before fracture healing.

candidates.title: What Do National Joint Replacement Registries Fail to Collect? The Critical Value of Recording Preoperative Alignment for Prediction of Revision After TKA: A Nested-model Analysis of Registry-only versus Seldom- and Never-recorded Variables.
candidates.authors_short: Hoskins W, Rosser K, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: National joint replacement registries inform prosthesis selection and health policy using a consistently recorded set of patient, implant, and surgical variables. However, preoperative radiographic alignment and detailed diagnostic complexity are rarely, if ever, captured. Surgeons pay close attention to limb alignment and deformity because both reflect the complexity of the knee being replaced and are associated with the risk of failure. However, the incremental value of recording these measurements, beyond the variables that registries already collect, has not been quantified. As preoperative alignment can be read from the same long-leg radiographs that many surgeons already obtain, even a small improvement in identifying which knees will be revised could justify the modest cost of recording it. QUESTIONS/PURPOSES: In a 15-year, single-center, TKA group with comprehensive preoperative alignment assessments and national joint replacement registry linkage, we asked: (1) How well do the variables that a national joint replacement registry routinely records identify which knees will later be revised (as quantified by a metric called discrimination, where 0.50 is no better than chance and 1.00 is perfect prediction)? (2) Does adding diagnostic-complexity variables improve that discrimination? (3) Does adding preoperative alignment variables improve it further? (4) When alignment is left out, by how much do the risk estimates that registries report for common surgical decisions (their HRs) change? METHODS: A retrospective analysis of 2341 primary TKAs in 1917 patients performed between January 2010 and May 2024 at a single tertiary center was conducted, all with national-registry linkage and a documented preoperative long-leg standing radiograph. The primary outcome was aseptic revision, modeled with nested Fine-Gray regression and death treated as a competing risk, meaning that a patient who dies can no longer be revised and is not simply removed from the denominator. To check that the findings were not an artifact of incomplete imaging, we repeated the entire analysis in a more completely imaged group (a prespecified sensitivity analysis), which was a subset of 1567 procedures with both preoperative and postoperative long-leg radiographs (the paired-imaging subset). We built the models (M) stepwise to determine how much each kind of information added. The M1 used the variables that a registry routinely records, M2 added three diagnostic-complexity variables, and M3 added three preoperative alignment variables. To measure how much each group of variables contributed, we compared neighboring models statistically, using an intermediate model (M2.5) to isolate the share attributable to limb alignment. We measured how well each model separated the knees that were later revised from those that were not using a score called the concordance index (C-index): 0.50 means that the model is no better than a coin toss, 1.00 means it is always right, and 0.66 means it ranks a revised knee above a nonrevised one about two-thirds of the time. Because any model flatters itself on the same knees that were used to build it, we also tested each model on knees it had not seen by rebuilding it on part of the data and checking it on the rest, repeatedly, keeping both knees of a patient together. That cross-validated C-index is the honest figure and the one we rely on. The in-sample figure is reported alongside it because earlier studies report it, and the gap between the two shows how much of the apparent gain is optimism rather than real predictive information. RESULTS: The registry-only variable set (M1) identified the risk of aseptic revision only modestly (apparent C-index 0.66 in the primary group and 0.67 in the sensitivity group; cross-validated 0.59 and 0.61). Adding diagnostic-complexity variables (M2) did not improve this. Adding preoperative alignment (M3) raised apparent discrimination to 0.68 in the primary group and 0.69 in the sensitivity group, but it did not improve cross-validated discrimination in either. Taking everything the models added from M1 to M3, that addition was detectable as a whole only in the sensitivity group, not in the primary group. Within it, limb alignment carried most of the information in the sensitivity group (68%; p < 0.001) and about half of it in the primary group (47%; p = 0.02); diagnostic complexity accounted for the remainder (31% and 52%) but could not be distinguished from the effects of chance, and the knee-specific angles added nothing detectable in either (1%). In the full model, the preoperative mechanical hip-knee-ankle angle was associated with aseptic revision in the sensitivity group (subdistribution HR 1.06 for each degree, the angle entered as its signed difference from 180°, where 180° is a straight limb, < 180° is varus, and > 180° is valgus [95% confidence interval (CI) 1.00 to 1.12]; p = 0.03); the same association was present but not statistically distinguishable from the effects of chance in the primary group (subdistribution HR 1.04 [95% CI 0.99 to 1.09]; p = 0.11). Leaving alignment out changed some registry-style HRs. For example, the HR for tibial stem use shifted by 17% in the primary group. The findings were consistent, and stronger, in the more completely imaged subset (n = 1567; 68 revisions). When alignment was added, about 30% of knees in the primary group and 34% in the subset moved into a different third of predicted risk. CONCLUSION: The variables that registries routinely record identify the risk of aseptic TKA revision only modestly. Preoperative limb alignment adds a small but consistent and clinically interpretable amount of predictive information, and it is stronger in the subset of knees for which both preoperative and postoperative imaging existed, although we did not test postoperative alignment as a predictor in its own right. Leaving alignment out also shifts the registry-style HRs that surgeons and policymakers rely on for some surgical decisions. Registries should therefore consider recording at least one preoperative alignment field. In practice, this could begin as a simple category (varus, neutral, or valgus) read from films that surgeons already obtain, beginning as a pilot before any wider rollout, because even partial recording would add value. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: 2025 ICM updated evidence-based definition of shoulder PJI from multicenter Delphi process directly standardizes diagnosis for all shoulder arthroplasty surgeons globally.
bullets: Registry variables alone predict TKA revision only modestly, and adding preoperative limb alignment improved risk classification for roughly one-third of knees.
For any patient undergoing primary TKA, preoperative mechanical alignment carries clinically meaningful predictive information that current registries do not capture.
Omitting preoperative alignment distorts registry-reported risk estimates for implant choices, such as tibial stem use, by up to 17%, affecting decisions surgeons and policymakers rely on.

candidates.title: Evolving Management Strategies for Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus: A Contemporary Treatment Algorithm.
candidates.authors_short: Rubin J, Tham A, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume
candidates.abstract: ➢ Osteochondral lesions of the talus (OLT) are common injuries that remain difficult to treat because of the challenge of restoring durable hyaline cartilage. Surgical outcomes are influenced by lesion size and morphology, cartilage integrity, subchondral bone involvement, and ankle stability, all of which should be considered when evaluating operative strategies.➢ Fragment fixation preserves the native osteochondral unit in lesions with a viable fragment and is primarily indicated in acute OLT. Lift-drill-fill-fix is utilized in selected chronic lesions with a salvageable fragment and compromised subchondral bone, allowing restoration of the lesion bed and stable fixation.➢ Bone marrow stimulation techniques, including microfracture, antegrade drilling, and retrograde drilling, have demonstrated improvements in pain and functional outcomes in small and contained lesions, although the long-term durability of fibrocartilaginous repair tissue remains variable.➢ Replacement procedures such as autologous osteochondral transplantation and osteochondral allograft transplantation restore the osteochondral unit and have demonstrated favorable outcomes in larger or structurally complex lesions. Cell-based and matrix-assisted cartilage restoration strategies, such as autologous chondrocyte implantation, matrix-induced autologous chondrocyte implantation, and autologous matrix-induced chondrogenesis, have demonstrated improvements in clinical outcomes and cartilage repair in selected patients with OLT.➢ Emerging restorative approaches such as scaffold-based cartilage repair, osteoperiostic autografting techniques, and biologic adjuncts including concentrated bone marrow aspirate, platelet-rich plasma, and hyaluronic acid have demonstrated promising early clinical results, although current evidence remains limited.➢ Salvage procedures, including bulk allograft transplantation, metallic resurfacing, hemiarthroplasty, and arthrodesis, may be considered for extensive lesions or after failure of prior surgical management, although outcomes remain variable, with high complication and failure rates.
candidates.score_reasoning: JBJS instructional review on cervical disc arthroplasty with RCT-level evidence synthesis provides comprehensive, clinically actionable guidance for cervical spine surgeons.
bullets: Lesion size, fragment viability, subchondral bone status, and ankle stability should guide surgical decision-making for osteochondral lesions of the talus.
Bone marrow stimulation works for small contained lesions, while osteochondral transplantation produces better results for larger or structurally complex lesions.
Salvage procedures including bulk allograft, metallic resurfacing, and arthrodesis carry high complication and failure rates and should be reserved for extensive lesions or failed prior surgery.

candidates.title: Is Routine Patellar Resurfacing During Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty Associated With Increased Rates of Postoperative Peripatellar Injury?
candidates.authors_short: Dundon JM, Lewis S, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Routine patellar resurfacing during primary total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is common in the United States. Complications to the peripatellar area and extensor mechanism following TKA are rare but catastrophic. The purpose of this study was to investigate the association between routine patellar resurfacing during primary TKA and rates of postoperative peripatellar injury requiring operative treatment. METHODS: This was a retrospective, single, high-volume practice cohort study of 3383 consecutive primary TKAs between June 2023 and April 2025. Surgical data including surgeon, performance of routine patellar resurfacing, and type of peripatellar surgery performed were collected. Data analysis was analyzed using Fisher's exact test, and statistical significance was defined as a P value less than 0.05. RESULTS: There were 2508 knees in the resurfaced patella group and 875 knees in the non-resurfaced patella group. All peripatellar injuries (22) occurred in the patellar resurfaced group (0.88%; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.55% to 1.33%). No patients underwent surgical treatment of patellar fracture. In the routine non-resurfaced group, 0 patients underwent peripatellar repair surgery (0%; 95% CI, 0% to 0.42%), corresponding to an absolute risk difference of 0.88 percentage points (P value = .002). Firth regression produced an odds ratio of 15.85 (profile 95% CI, 2.20 to 2013.54; P = .0015). CONCLUSION: In this retrospective single-practice cohort, operatively treated peripatellar injuries were observed only among resurfaced knees. Although a statistically significant association was identified, the absolute event rate was low. Longer-term data are required to determine the rates of overall revision between the 2 groups.
candidates.score_reasoning: CORR prospective study using weightbearing CT and 3D shape modeling to evaluate AFO effectiveness in CMT cavovarus deformity, providing novel objective data for a common orthotic decision.
bullets: In a series of 3,383 primary total knee arthroplasties, all 22 peripatellar injuries requiring surgery occurred in resurfaced knees, with zero in the non-resurfaced group.
Patients undergoing routine patellar resurfacing carried an absolute risk of operative peripatellar injury near 1%, a risk not seen in those whose patella was left unresurfaced.

For orthopaedic surgeons performing primary total knee arthroplasty, this data supports reconsidering routine patellar resurfacing, though long-term revision rates between the two groups remain unknown.
